children: 0719 GMT - Bitcoin rises modestly following gains on Wall Street overnight driven by a rally in tech stocks. Investors buying shares of companies tied to artificial intelligence boosted tech stocks, leading U.S. stock indices higher. An easing of oil prices is also supporting risk sentiment. Lower oil prices reflect some profit taking and reports that Saudi Arabia could soon restore some flows through its damaged East-West pipeline which was closed after a drone attack from Iraq. Bitcoin rises 1.1% to $77,392, LSEG data show. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0656 GMT - Sterling rises slightly after data showed U.K. retail sales unexpectedly returned to growth in August. Sales rose 0.5% in August compared to the previous month, beating the 0.1% decline expected by economists in a WSJ survey. It follows an unrevised 0.5% decrease in sales in July. The data come after the Bank of England voted 6-3 to leave interest rates at 3.75% Thursday but delivered tentative signals about raising rates in future. Sterling rises 0.1% to $1.3370 after the data, from $1.3361 beforehand. The euro trades steady at 0.8585 pounds, compared to 0.8590 before the data. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0652 GMT - The dollar trades steady, close to a multiweek high against a basket of currencies, as the Japanese yen falls after a split vote by the Bank of Japan to raise interest rates Friday cast doubt over further policy tightening. The BOJ increased its policy rate to 1.25%, as expected, in a 7-2 vote. The yen's negative reaction also reflects some speculation that the BOJ could have delivered a jumbo rate rise and because the central bank doesn't sound ready for back-to-back tightening, Danske Bank analysts say in a note. The decision follows the Federal Reserve's unanimous vote Wednesday to raise rates. The DXY dollar index rises 0.1% to 100.289, near Thursday's seven-week high of 100.367. The dollar rises 0.5% to 156.66 yen. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0637 GMT - If Japan's inflation settles near 2%, the 10-year Japanese government bond yield of 3% seems reasonable, says Citi Research strategist Tomohisa Fujiki. "Yields could rise further, depending on future rate hikes and crude price dynamics," he says. "However, if the policy rate does not rise above 2%, a 3% yield should be attractive for real money investors," he adds. While the market is expected to price in roughly quarterly rate hikes for the time being, Japan's terminal rate is likely to be capped at or below 2%, Fujiki says. The 10-year JGB yield is last down 1.5 basis points at 2.975%.(megumi.fujikawa@wsj.com)

0615 GMT - Taiwan's central bank could keep monetary policy unchanged in December but begin hiking in 1Q 2027 if inflationary pressures persist, Commerzbank Research analysts say in a note. Gov. Yang Chin-long this week struck a patient tone, noting that "inflation is still under control, so we have time to wait and see," saying its monetary policy "remains on the tight side for now." His comments suggest that the central bank sees little urgency to tighten, as the current stance is sufficiently restrictive to contain inflation. However, the policy statement also signals that policymakers remain mindful of rising inflation risks from external factors, including higher global oil prices and U.S. trade policy uncertainty. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0610 GMT - The Bank of Japan's policy statement released Friday signals that the bank will likely maintain a faster pace than the timeline of hiking roughly twice a year, which had been expected by markets previously, says Daiwa Securities economist Kento Minami. "The key is the [BOJ's] assessment that financial conditions will remain accommodative even after the policy interest rate change," Minami says. Although Friday's rate hike pushed the policy rate above the lower bound of the BOJ's estimated neutral interest rate range of 1.1% to 2.5%, the bank retains its view that monetary conditions are still easy, he adds. That provides grounds for the central bank to tighten monetary policy further. (megumi.fujikawa@wsj.com)

0555 GMT - Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's fundamentally cautious stance toward monetary tightening is likely to remain unchanged despite the Bank of Japan's faster-than-usual pace of interest-rate increases, say analysts at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities. BOJ board members Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato, both appointed by Takaichi, voted against Friday's rate hike. "The government's concerns that interest-rate increases could dampen corporate investment appetite and household spending are likely to stay largely intact," the analysts say. The yen weakened after the announcement, hovering near 157.20 per dollar as the vote split cast doubt on the pace of further policy tightening. (megumi.fujikawa@wsj.com)

0550 GMT - U.S. Treasury yields edge lower in Asian trade, as the Federal Reserve's interest-rate hike on Wednesday looks to have convinced investors about the Fed's intention to lower inflation back to target. "The medicine from the Fed is working and may have prevented the rates sell-off from spiraling out of control," Commerzbank's Rainer Guntermann says in a note. "Bond markets stabilize with curves flattening amid lower long-end yields," the rates strategist says. The two-year Treasury yield is down 0.7 basis point at 4.681%, while the 10-year Treasury yield declines 1 basis point to 4.935%, according to Tradeweb. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0546 GMT - The U.S. Treasury's expanded long-end bond buybacks appear to have had limited success in lowering outright yields, but they have left a clear footprint in relative-value pricing at the long end, Deutsche Bank rates strategists say in a note. Since the Aug. 19 announcement, the 20-year maturity sector has outperformed both on the curve and in swap spreads, with these effects persisting even as long-end yields have risen above their preannouncement levels, they say. "The key reason is the 20-year sector's relative illiquidity and weaker investor demand, which leave greater scope for expanded buybacks to support valuations," they say. Another reason is the smaller 20-year issuance size, with just $168 billion annually compared with $480 billion for 10-year notes and $276 billion for 30-year bonds, they add. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0535 GMT - A local peak in long-end yields may be behind us, but the next one is likely still ahead, Societe Generale rates strategists say in a note. "A hawkish European Central Bank and Federal Reserve should reassure investors questioning central banks' inflation-fighting credibility," they say. The Bank of England's decision to pause and slow quantitative tightening sparked a gilt-led rally at the long end, while next week's Trump-Xi meeting could further support risk sentiment, they say. "However, the global rebuilding of term premia is not yet complete, and markets still have scope to price a more aggressive path of central bank rate hikes," according to the French bank's rates strategists. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0533 GMT - Societe Generale rates strategists raise their forecasts for 10-year German Bund yields, as the rise in long-end yields is not over, they say in a note. They expect the 10-year Bund yields to peak around 3.85% in the first quarter of 2027, they say. Near term, the U.S.-Iran conflict and energy remain the key drivers and the source of uncertainty for rates and market pricing of the European Central Bank's rate path, they say. "The speed of the recent ECB repricing has surprised many market participants, but the level of the terminal rate can easily be rationalized," they say. The 10-year Bund yield closed at 3.478% on Thursday, according to LSEG. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0526 GMT - ​Edmond de Rothschild Asset Management views current interest-rate levels as an opportunity to strengthen its investments in rate assets, Michael Nizard, head of multi-asset and overlay says in a note. The asset manager thus moves to a significant overweight position in bonds--particularly those with short to medium maturities--with a view to generating carry returns and building its portfolio, Nizard says. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)
